en.title: THE SECOND URBANISATION
en.summary: The expression “second urbanisation” is commonly used for the growth of towns, cities, states, specialised production and long-distance exchange in northern India during the early first millennium BCE, especially in the Ganga plains. It is useful only if it is not turned into a fixed date or a single-cause event.

mai.title: दोसरा नगरीकरण
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “दोसरा नगरीकरण” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Scope: “second urbanisation” is a shorthand, not a single event
What makes the process “second”
The Middle Ganga plain was not empty before cities
Iron mattered, but it was not an urban switch

en.title: HOUSEHOLD AND FAMILY IN EARLY HISTORIC SOCIETY
en.summary: A history of family cannot begin by assuming that every person lived in a nuclear family, a “joint family,” or a fixed patrilineage. These are analytical labels, not archaeological finds. A household is first of all a unit of co-residence, provisioning, labour and care; family describes relationships created through birth, marriage, adoption and social recognition; lineage refers to descent remembered across generations; and political clan membership may operate at a still larger scale.

mai.title: आरम्भिक ऐतिहासिक समाजमे घर-परिवार
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “आरम्भिक ऐतिहासिक समाजमे घर-परिवार” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Scope: household, family and lineage are not synonyms
The evidence problem is unusually severe
Domestic architecture is evidence for co-residence, not a family tree
Household archaeology works through repeated activity

en.title: SOCIAL DIFFERENTIATION BEFORE FIXED CASTE NARRATIVES
en.summary: Early historic society in the Middle Ganga valley was unequal, but inequality should not be reconstructed by placing every person into a later, fully elaborated caste order. Political rank, control of land and labour, ritual prestige, occupation, lineage, gender, wealth, freedom or dependency, and access to institutions could all shape social position. These axes overlapped, yet they did not always coincide.

mai.title: स्थिर जाति-कथासँ पहिने सामाजिक भिन्नता
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “स्थिर जाति-कथासँ पहिने सामाजिक भिन्नता” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Scope: differentiation is not the same as a finished caste system
The sources speak in different social vocabularies
Social position worked through several overlapping axes
Varṇa was a powerful classificatory ideal, not a demographic spreadsheet

en.title: WOMEN IN EARLY MITHILA–VAJJI–ANGA
en.summary: Women in the early historic societies of Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be reconstructed as a single, uniform social category. The surviving evidence is uneven and genre-bound: archaeology reveals households, production, consumption and inequality but seldom identifies gender securely; Buddhist and Jain texts preserve named women and institutional debates but are literary and religious compositions; Brahmanical normative texts prescribe marriage, inheritance and conduct rather than recording every local practice.

mai.title: आरम्भिक मिथिला-वज्जि-अंगमे महिला
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “आरम्भिक मिथिला-वज्जि-अंगमे महिला” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Scope: women were differentiated by more than gender
The source problem is especially acute for women
Regional evidence is uneven: Vesālī is unusually visible
Household labour is fundamental but archaeologically difficult to gender

en.title: AGRICULTURE AND THE RURAL ECONOMY
en.summary: Agriculture sustained the demographic, urban and institutional transformations discussed in the preceding chapters, but the rural economy cannot be reduced to a single image of the timeless Indian village. In the Middle Ganga plains, cultivation was embedded in floodplain ecology, seasonal rainfall, livestock, household labour, storage, exchange, political extraction and religious patronage. The evidence is uneven.

mai.title: कृषि आ ग्रामीण अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “कृषि आ ग्रामीण अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Scope: the rural economy was historical, not timeless
Evidence must be matched to the claim
Agrarian intensification had a long prehistory
Rice was central, but the countryside was not a rice monoculture

en.title: CRAFTS AND TECHNOLOGY
en.summary: Craft history asks how knowledge, materials, labour and exchange were combined to make useful and valued objects. The archaeological record of Mithila, Vajji and Anga preserves pottery, metal tools, ornaments, beads, terracottas, bone and ivory objects, bricks and other durable remains, but it preserves wood, fibre, leather and many workshop installations much less reliably. The presence of a finished knife, bead or fine pot therefore cannot automatically be converted into proof of a local workshop.

mai.title: शिल्प आ प्रौद्योगिकी
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “शिल्प आ प्रौद्योगिकी” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Technology was social knowledge, not a list of inventions
A finished object does not prove a workshop
Craft specialisation existed in degrees
Pottery was the largest surviving craft archive

en.title: Trade, Merchants and Markets
en.summary: Chapter argument. Trade in early Mithila–Vajji–Aṅga is best reconstructed as a set of overlapping local, regional and long-distance exchanges rather than as one integrated “market economy.” Archaeology establishes movement of materials and objects; early Buddhist and Jain texts reveal categories of merchants, journeys and transactions; rivers and roads supplied the spatial infrastructure; and urban centres such as Vaiśālī and Campā concentrated demand, craft production, finance and redistribution.

mai.title: व्यापार, व्यापारी आ बजार
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “व्यापार, व्यापारी आ बजार” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Trade must be reconstructed from converging evidence
Exchange was older than cities and broader than formal markets
Agrarian surplus and commerce were mutually dependent
Rivers were transport corridors, resource zones and risk environments

en.title: Vaishali as an Economic and Social Centre
en.summary: Chapter argument. Vaiśālī should be understood neither as a literary city of splendour detached from archaeology nor as an excavated mound that can be interpreted without texts. Its historical importance lies in the convergence of a large early historic settlement, political institutions associated with the Licchavis and Vajji, a diversified material economy, regional routes, and unusually rich Buddhist and Jain memories. The evidence does not support a single census-like reconstruction of the city.

mai.title: आर्थिक आ सामाजिक केन्द्र रूपमे वैशाली
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “आर्थिक आ सामाजिक केन्द्र रूपमे वैशाली” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: An urban centre must be reconstructed from several evidence streams
Vaiśālī was a distributed urban landscape rather than a single compact monument
The city is an archaeological palimpsest
NBPW belongs to a wider urban transformation, not to a uniquely Vaiśālian culture

en.title: Anga and Champa
en.summary: Chapter argument. Aṅga and its capital Campā must be reconstructed through a controlled combination of archaeology, early Buddhist and Jain textual traditions, river geography, and later historical testimony. Campā was not simply a literary “great city” or a modern place-name attached to Bhagalpur. Excavation near Nathnagar–Champanagar documents a fortified and repeatedly rebuilt settlement with Northern Black Polished Ware, ring-wells, coins, sealings, craft objects and structural remains.

mai.title: अंग आ चम्पा
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “अंग आ चम्पा” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Aṅga is a historical region, not a synonym for the modern Bhagalpur district
The identification of ancient Campā with the Bhagalpur–Nathnagar landscape rests on converging evidence
Campā’s river setting was an economic asset and an archaeological complication
Fortification indicates collective investment, defence and boundary-making

en.title: Early money and monetisation
en.summary: Chapter argument. Early money in Mithilā, Vajji and Aṅga should be reconstructed as a layered history of measurement, portable value, coin manufacture, circulation, credit and institutional payment rather than as a simple transition from barter to cash. Silver punch-marked and copper coins widened the possibilities of exchange, taxation and saving, but their presence does not prove that all transactions were monetised.

mai.title: आरम्भिक मुद्रा आ मौद्रीकरण
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “आरम्भिक मुद्रा आ मौद्रीकरण” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Monetisation is not synonymous with the appearance of coins
Before coinage, value could already be measured, transferred and owed
Five evidence streams are needed to reconstruct early money
The beginning of Indian coinage remains a chronological problem, not a single secure date

en.title: Buddhist and Jain institutional economies
en.summary: Chapter argument. Buddhist and Jain communities in the early eastern Ganga plain should be understood as institutions that reorganised material dependence rather than escaped the economy. Renunciants limited private possession and ordinary production, yet their food, robes, lodging, medicine, travel, buildings and teaching required durable support relationships.

mai.title: बौद्ध आ जैन संस्थागत अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “बौद्ध आ जैन संस्थागत अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Institutional economy means organised material dependence, not a claim that religion was “really business”
Five evidence streams must be kept distinct before they are combined
Renunciation increased dependence on society rather than eliminating economic relations
The Buddhist “four requisites” reveal the material minimum of monastic life

en.title: Education, debate and intellectual communities
en.summary: Chapter argument. Education in early Videha, Vajji and Aṅga was not a single “school system” and should not be reconstructed by projecting later universities or medieval scholastic institutions into the first millennium BCE. Knowledge moved through households, teacher–pupil lineages, courts, ritual specialists, renunciant communities, urban audiences and mobile networks.

mai.title: शिक्षा, वाद-विवाद आ बौद्धिक समुदाय
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “शिक्षा, वाद-विवाद आ बौद्धिक समुदाय” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Education is a social relationship before it is a building
Five evidence streams must be separated before they are combined
Oral transmission was a technology of precision, not a primitive absence of writing
The teacher–pupil household linked learning to kinship, service and discipline

en.title: Health, medicine and the body
en.summary: Chapter argument. Health in early Mithilā–Videha, Vajji and Aṅga must be reconstructed from bodily vulnerability, care relationships, urban infrastructure, monastic regulation, specialist healing and the environmental conditions of dense settlement. The chapter does not project classical Āyurveda backward as a fully formed regional system, diagnose ancient populations from modern disease maps, or turn wells and drains into evidence for hospitals.

mai.title: स्वास्थ्य, चिकित्सा आ देह
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “स्वास्थ्य, चिकित्सा आ देह” विषयक आरम्भिक नगरीकरण, परिवार, सामाजिक भिन्नता, कृषि, शिल्प, बजार आ संस्थानक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Health history begins with bodies under constraint, not with a timeless medical system
Five evidence streams must remain separate before synthesis
Archaeology is strongest for environments of health, weakest for named disease
Illness disrupted labour, ritual and mobility and therefore had economic effects
